title: I Have Seen Your Face, as One Sees the Face of God — the Embrace, the Gift, the Tent
blocks: Peace be with you, brothers and sisters. Today I would like you to begin by opening, in your mind, the contacts list on your phone, and scrolling slowly down it. Somewhere down that list there is a name where your finger will pause for a moment — and then skip past. That name might be a member of your family. It might be a co-worker you once served alongside. It might be someone who wronged you back then, or someone you wronged. He comes into your mind often enough. But that call has still never been made.

And the reason we have not made it is usually not that we forgot. It is that we have already written the script for the other person. In the script he is cold. In the script he drags up everything from years ago. In the script he says one sentence that keeps you awake for three nights. We have read that script a few hundred times, until we believe it ourselves. And then we tell ourselves: never mind, time heals everything. But time has never yet healed a single relationship that was left unattended. All it does is bury it deeper.

Genesis chapter 33 is the day Jacob made that call. He had been afraid all night long — he divided the company, he prepared a present, he prayed, and then he wrestled a round with God, and the socket of his thigh has him limping still. He had run every worst-case script there is. And in the end the real point of that day was not anything he had prepared. It was that his brother came running out from among those four hundred men, fell on his neck, and the two of them wept.
1. He Divided the Company, and Put the Ones He Loved Most at the Back

The chapter opens like this: "Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants. He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear." (Genesis 33:1–2)
This is an uncomfortable passage to read. Because it sets out one father's partiality in a line, in plain view, for anyone at all to count.

Standing at the very front, in the most dangerous position, are the two servants and their children. Standing in the middle are Leah and her six children. Standing at the very back, in the safest position of all, are Rachel and Joseph.

Brothers and sisters, that one line-up laid out thirty years of family trouble in advance. Why did Joseph's brothers hate him? It did not begin with that coat of many colours. It began on this day. The moment they were made to stand at the front, they saw exactly where they came in their father's heart. Children never learn from what you say. They learn from how you line them up.

And notice the timing. Only last night he wrestled with God; only last night he was given the new name Israel. A person can have a real encounter with God and still wake up the next morning with the old fault entirely intact. Grace arrives in a moment; change is a road you walk.
This is the honesty of Scripture. It writes Jacob's tears of last night and Jacob's favouritism of this morning side by side, on the same page.
But verse 3 brings a turn: "He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother."

He arranged the line and put his family in front of him as a shield — and then he walked out to the very front himself. In twenty years, this is the first time Jacob has ever put himself in the most dangerous place.

"Bowed himself to the ground seven times" is not a loose turn of phrase. It is the highest courtesy a subject of the ancient Near East could pay a king; in the clay-tablet letters unearthed at Amarna in Egypt, a vassal king greets Pharaoh with exactly this — "at the feet of my lord I fall down seven times and seven times." Jacob paid the honours due to a king, in order to meet the brother he had once cheated.

Once he grabbed; today he bows. Once he sent other people out ahead of him; today he goes out ahead of them. Whether a man's repentance is real is not measured by how loudly he weeps. It is measured by whether his order of things has been turned around.
He was given a new name only last night, and by this morning he is putting the ones he loves most at the back. Does that mean the change did not take?

Scripture writes last night's tears and this morning's favouritism side by side on the same page, and that is precisely its honesty. Hold two things apart: grace arrives in a moment, change is a road you walk. That night God really did touch him — but twenty years of ingrained partiality does not vanish in a single morning. This is an enormous release for us, and it is also a very serious warning. The release is this: if you have had a genuine encounter and you still fall, that does not make the encounter a lie. The warning is this: never let one night of being moved stand in for a lifetime of practice. The real evidence is not how hard you wept that night. It is whether, in the days that follow, the order of things slowly gets turned around.
Did that line-up really cause trouble later on?

It is very likely the source of the tragedy in chapter 37. Joseph's brothers hated him, and most people remember only the coat — but the coat is not where it started. It started on this day, when they stood at the front, in the most dangerous place, and saw with their own eyes what number they came in their father's heart. Children never learn from what you say; they learn from how you line them up. And that is intensely practical for parents: saying "I treat you all the same" achieves nothing at all. Your children will remember who sat next to you, whose event you took a day off work for, and whose mistakes you made excuses for. If you want that to change, start by changing one concrete arrangement.
2. A Light from the Original: Last Night He Lifted His Hands, This Morning He Lifts His Eyes

There is a word in verse 1 that stitches chapter 32 and chapter 33 together. "Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked" — in Hebrew that is וַיִּשָּׂא עֵינָיו (*vayisa einav*), literally "he lifted up his eyes."

Last night, what Jacob lifted was his hands — he held on to that man and would not let go, saying, "I won't let you go unless you bless me." This morning, what he lifts is his eyes. The hand that clutched and would not let go has become the eyes that look up and see; and between the two lie one night of wrestling and one crippled leg.

And that word "divided" at the head of the chapter — in Hebrew וַיַּחַץ (*vayachats*) — is the same verb used in 32:7, where in his terror he "divided the people who were with him … into two companies." Last night's fear is still there in his hands this morning. People do not stop being afraid the moment they have finished praying. People carry the fear along with them, and walk forward anyway.
Verse 4 has four verbs running one after another with no room to breathe in between: "Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept."
"Ran" is וַיָּרָץ (*vayarats*). In the world of the Old Testament an elder with standing does not run; to run is to lose face. Esau ran, because it was his brother.

"Fell on his neck" is וַיִּפֹּל עַל־צַוָּארָו, literally "he fell upon his neck." Luke 15:20 says of the prodigal's father, "But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him" — and the Greek Old Testament uses exactly that same set of words right here.
Brothers and sisters, when the Lord Jesus told the parable of the prodigal son, he had Genesis 33 in his hand. There is a shadow of Esau on that father who came running.

"Kissed him" is וַיִּשָּׁקֵהוּ. In chapter 27, Isaac said to Jacob, who was impersonating Esau, "Come near now, and kiss me, my son" — and there was deception hidden inside that kiss. Inside this one, nothing is hidden. And the verb behind "they wept" is plural, וַיִּבְכּוּ — the tears of reconciliation are never one-sided.

The order of events here is worth kneeling down to think about. Jacob was afraid for a whole night and set aside more than five hundred head of livestock; Esau did not so much as look at the livestock first. While Jacob was still counting sheep, God had long since been at work inside Esau's heart.

We generally assume that reconciliation is something we negotiate for ourselves. In fact the very ordeal you are dreading is one God has often already walked through inside the other person's heart. Your part matters, and you must do it — but your part has never been the decisive one.
"Bowed himself to the ground seven times" — is that not lowering himself much too far?

It is the highest courtesy a subject of the ancient Near East could pay a king; in the clay-tablet letters unearthed at Amarna in Egypt, a vassal king greets Pharaoh with precisely this — "at the feet of my lord I fall down seven times and seven times." So yes, he really did pay the honours due to a king in order to meet the brother he had once cheated. But notice one thing: he was able to bow because he had already bowed before God the night before. A head bowed before people, with no surrender before God underneath it, will sour sooner or later and turn into resentment. So the way to judge whether an apology is real is not how low the posture goes. It is whether the man first owned the matter before God.
Esau "ran" over and embraced him. What is special about that action?

In the world of the Old Testament an elder with standing does not run; to run is to lose face. Esau ran, because it was his brother. And "fell on his neck" is literally "he fell upon his neck" — in Luke 15 the prodigal's father "ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him", and the Greek Old Testament uses exactly that same set of words. When the Lord Jesus told the parable of the prodigal son, he had Genesis 33 in his hand. And this gives us a very deep comfort: while Jacob was still counting sheep and getting his present ready, God had long since been at work inside Esau's heart.
3. I Have Seen Your Face, as One Sees the Face of God
Esau asks, "Who are these with you?" (Genesis 33:5). The Hebrew is מִי־אֵלֶּה לָּךְ, literally "who are these to you?" He is not asking for a head count. He is asking about a relationship.

Jacob answers, "The children whom God has graciously given your servant." "Graciously given" is חָנַן (*chanan*), a favour handed over for nothing, from the same root as "favour", חֵן. For the first time in twenty years, Jacob puts everything in his household down to God's account rather than to his own manoeuvring.

Esau says, "I have enough, my brother; let that which you have be yours." (Genesis 33:9) After twenty years he finally calls him אָחִי — my brother. The last time he spoke of Jacob, back in chapter 27, it was to say, "Then I will kill my brother Jacob." The same word, at a completely different temperature.
And then comes the summit of the whole chapter: "I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me." (Genesis 33:10)

"Your face" is פָּנֶיךָ; "the face of God" is פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים. Last night Jacob named that place Peniel (פְּנִיאֵל), which means exactly "the face of God." This morning, on his brother's face, he sees it a second time.

Brothers and sisters, this is the weightiest sentence about reconciliation in the whole Bible. What it says is this: a face that is willing to forgive makes a person think of the face of God. In the moment you forgive somebody, you have stood in front of him and been, for that moment, the face of God. And the reverse holds just as well — a face that will never forgive blocks another person's way to knowing God.

There is one more word here that is easy to read straight past. In verse 11 Jacob says, "Please take the gift that I brought to you" — and the word behind "gift" here is no longer מִנְחָה, the word the previous chapter used. It is בִּרְכָתִי — "my blessing."

Twenty years ago, what he cheated out of this brother's hands was precisely that blessing — Esau wept that day and said, "See, now he has taken away my blessing." Today, with his own hands, Jacob sends "my blessing" back.

That is called restitution. Repentance does not finish with one apology; repentance is giving back what you took all those years ago, as much of it as can be given back. Zacchaeus said, "If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much" — and then the Lord Jesus said, "Today, salvation has come to this house."

And the reason he dares to give it back is a sentence he says first: "God has dealt graciously with me, and … I have enough." The Hebrew is יֶשׁ־לִי־כֹל, literally "I have everything." Compare the two brothers. Esau says, "I have plenty" (רָב). Jacob says, "I have everything."

Only a person who knows that in God he has everything is able to give anything away. People who cannot give are usually not stingy. They are people who feel, deep inside, that they do not have enough.
"I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God" — does a sentence like that not lift a human being far too high?

Last night Jacob named that place Peniel, which means exactly "the face of God"; this morning, on his brother's face, he sees it a second time. The sentence is not treating a man as God. It is saying this: a face that is willing to forgive makes a person think of the face of God. And the reverse holds just as well — a face that will never forgive blocks another person's way to knowing God. That is a heavy reminder for every believer: in the moment you forgive somebody, you have stood in front of him and been, for that moment, the face of God; and if you are holding on to an account you will not let go of, then you are painting a false face of God for him to look at.
Jacob says, "Please take the gift that I brought to you." Is there something hidden in the word "gift" here?

There is. In this verse the Hebrew is no longer מִנְחָה, a present, the word the previous chapter used. It is בִּרְכָתִי — "my blessing." Twenty years ago what he cheated out of this brother's hands was precisely that blessing; Esau wept that day and said, "See, now he has taken away my blessing." Today, with his own hands, Jacob sends "my blessing" back. That is called restitution. Repentance does not finish with one apology; repentance is giving back what you took, as much of it as can be given back — Zacchaeus said, "If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much", and only then did the Lord Jesus say, "Today, salvation has come to this house." In practical terms you can ask yourself one question: what did I take out of somebody's hands back then — an opportunity, a reputation, a sum of money, a word of affirmation I owed and never gave — and is there still some way today to give part of it back?
4. He Said He Was Going to Seir, and He Went to Succoth
By this point the story is complete and rounded off. But the Bible does not put down its pen.

Esau says, "Let's take our journey, and let's go, and I will go before you." Jacob declines, and his reason is a moving one: "My lord knows that the children are tender, and that the flocks and herds with me have their young, and if they overdrive them one day, all the flocks will die … I will lead on gently, according to the pace of the livestock that are before me and according to the pace of the children." (Genesis 33:12–14)

"According to the pace" is לְרֶגֶל, literally "according to the foot of" — walking at the speed of the slowest one there. And "lead on gently" is נָהַל (*nahal*), the very word of Psalm 23, "He leads me beside still waters" — the verb for a shepherd gently guiding a flock.

This is the loveliest pastoral principle in the chapter: the speed of a community is not set by its strongest member; it is set by its weakest. If a church walks at the pace of its most capable people, there will be dead sheep along the road. And a family is exactly the same.
But — he says, "until I come to my lord to Seir." (Genesis 33:14)
Verse 17: "Jacob traveled to Succoth." Succoth lies east of the Jordan; Seir lies to the south. He said he was going south, and he went north. The directions are opposite.

I will not go so far as to say that Jacob lied. The text offers no comment, and I am not going to supply one on its behalf. But this crack has been deliberately left there unmended, and there must be a reason for that.

What deserves even more attention is the second half of verse 17: he "built himself a house." This is the first time a patriarch stops living in tents and puts up a house instead. Hebrews 11 says that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were "dwelling in tents", because "they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one." A tent can strike camp at any hour. A house cannot.
Then verse 18: "Jacob came in peace to the city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Paddan Aram; and encamped before the city."

"In peace" is שָׁלֵם (*shalem*), from the same root as "peace", שָׁלוֹם, and it means whole, undamaged, with not one thing missing. Back in chapter 28, at Bethel, God promised him that he would "come again to my father's house in peace", and this verse is the echo of that promise — God keeps his word, and not one syllable of it has been dropped.

But listen carefully. What God said was "come again to my father's house"; and by chapter 35 God has to say it once again: "Arise, go up to Bethel, and live there." Shechem is not Bethel. From Shechem to Bethel is barely thirty kilometres further on.

There he built an altar, and called it El Elohe Israel (אֵל אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל), which means "the Mighty One is the God of Israel." In the whole Old Testament this is the only altar named in that way. This is real worship. It is not a sham.
But a real altar, put up in a place where he should never have stopped, becomes the address of the tragedy that overtakes Dinah in the very next chapter.

Brothers and sisters, the most dangerous thing is usually not taking the wrong road. It is being nearly there. It is when we are nearly there that we are most likely to stop. And that last thirty kilometres is very often the place God actually meant to bring us.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot
This chapter is easy to preach movingly, and just as easy to preach crookedly. There are several places we absolutely must be able to recognise.

The first distortion is preaching reconciliation as though it always ends happily. This chapter has an embrace and it has tears — but in the same book, Jacob and Laban get no further than Mizpah, where they pile up a heap of stones and say, "I will not pass over this heap to you, and … you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, for harm." That is Scripture too. If we preach this as a formula — just be willing to bow first, and the other party is certain to come running — then the person who has been trying for ten years and still gets no reply to his messages will walk out convinced that the fault is that he is not good enough. The test is this: when the people whose relationships are still unmended have heard you, are they comforted, or are they condemned?

The second distortion is presenting Esau as a model of complete transformation. The text records the embrace of that one day; it tells us nothing about his faith afterwards, and Hebrews 12 still calls him a "profane person". We may say that God used Esau on that day. We may not write a testimony for Esau that Esau never wrote for himself. The test is this: are you preaching what the text says, or what you imagined?

The third distortion is skipping over the fact that Jacob never went to Seir, and never went up to Bethel either. Skip that crack and the congregation will assume that once you have been reconciled everything is fine. What the text wants us to see is a man who has been reconciled and is still out on the road. The test is this: as the congregation walks out, what have they seen — a perfect ending, or a man God is still leading?

The fourth distortion is preaching those seven bows as "get your posture low enough and it will work out." If bowing is a technique, it is only another way of grabbing. Jacob was able to bow because he had already bowed before God the night before. A head bowed before people, with no surrender before God underneath it, will sour sooner or later and turn into resentment.

The fifth distortion is taking "lead on gently, according to the pace" and using it to endorse your own stagnation. Slowing down for the slowest sheep is love; refusing to move at all is laziness. The way to tell them apart is one question: whom am I slowing down for?
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question. In our culture elders rarely apologise, and it is awkward for the younger generation to raise a thing first. So the cracks in a great many families are held together by simply not mentioning it — at New Year everyone still eats together, still puts food into one another's bowls, and that one matter has gone twenty years without a word. We call it "harmony above all". But the reconciliation of chapter 33 does not run on silence. It runs on Jacob walking out to the very front of the line himself, and putting the blessing he took all those years ago back into his brother's hands with his own hands. Brothers and sisters, not mentioning it is not forgiveness. Not mentioning it only covers the abscess over. If you are the younger one, you do not have to wait for your elder to speak first — in the text, the one who walks over first is precisely the one who did the wrong. And if you are the elder, you need to know this: the few steps you do not take, your children will spend a lifetime making up.

The second question. We are very good at using giving as a substitute for saying. We buy things, we put money in a red envelope, we send one more box of fruit — anything rather than get that sentence out of our mouths. Jacob too had prepared more than five hundred head of livestock, but those animals were not the reason the relationship was restored; the restoring began when Esau came running, and when Jacob said, "I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God." A gift can be an expression of love. It cannot be a stand-in for the sentence. So if you are going to send something over this week, write the sentence down first, and send it along with the gift.
I have already bowed first, and the other person still ignores me. Do I keep going?

First let us be clear about something: this chapter has an embrace and tears, but in the same book Jacob and Laban get no further than piling up a heap of stones at Mizpah. That is Scripture too. So do not preach reconciliation as a formula. In practice you can walk it like this. First, finish your own part — make the apology specific, give back what can be given back, and then stop. Second, hand the outcome over to God, and do not use message after message to force a response out of the other person; that turns into a different kind of pressure. Third, keep praying for him, and give yourself permission to live well while you wait. And if the other person is involved in ongoing harm or threat, keeping your distance is entirely legitimate.
7. Living 321 Out — Bow Before God First, and Only Then Before People
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model. Esau ran over and fell on his neck — the one who had been wronged closed the distance himself. That is exactly the shape of the cross: "But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Our role model is not "wait for him to apologise first." It is the One who came running first. So in my relationships, I will be the one who moves first.

The Bible is my standard. It is not my feelings saying "this person is not worth it"; it is Scripture saying, "If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men." Your feelings will tell you he is never going to change. The standard tells you to do your part. When the two of them collide, listen to the standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to speak, how to speak, whether to meet face to face — none of that is worked out by reasoning it through in your head. It comes from the guidance inside your heart. Rely on the intellect and rely on yourself, and you get worry; rely on the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit, and you get joy. It was only after God had touched Jacob at Peniel that he walked into Esau's arms.

Let Jesus be King. Jacob says, "God has dealt graciously with me, and … I have enough", and the Hebrew of it is "I have everything." A person who lets Jesus be King has his portion in Jesus, not in the other party's attitude; and so he is able to give, and able to give back. If you can only be well again once the other person apologises, then the throne of your life is still rented out to that person.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. The name of that altar is El Elohe Israel — the Mighty One is the God of Israel. On the day of the reconciliation, Jacob did not set up a pillar to commemorate his own wisdom and his own way with words. He built an altar. Everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus; in everything give thanks, and give him all the glory.

Establish God's system. This chapter shows us how a system gets broken, and it also shows us how one begins. It gets broken when you line your children up according to your favourites; it begins when you walk at the pace of the slowest sheep. And its greatest danger is stopping at Shechem — stopping because you are nearly there. To establish God's system is to walk that last thirty kilometres all the way to the end.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Embrace
Every one of us walks into this chapter carrying a different kind of heart.

The proud heart says, "He is the one who should be coming to me." You may genuinely be in the right; he may genuinely be the one who was wrong. But brothers and sisters, do you see it — in the text, the one who walks over first is the one in the wrong, and the one who comes running is the one in the right. Both of them moved, and so nobody was left standing where he was. If you keep waiting for a fair running order, that road will never be walked by anybody at all. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to sit in the judge's seat; humility is laying down that seat, returning to our originally intended position as human beings, and letting God be God.

The fearful heart says, "If I call him, he is certain to humiliate me." That was Jacob's state of mind for a whole night. He rehearsed the worst script a few hundred times, and in the end not one line of it was ever used. What fear does best is write other people's dialogue for them, and then believe it. Remember this: the ordeal you are dreading is one God has very often walked into ahead of you.

The ashamed heart says, "After what I did back then, I have no face to meet him with." Jacob had no face either — the people he cheated were his own father and his own brother. But he did not wait until he was clean before he went. He went with a limp. Shame tells you to hide; the gospel tells you to walk over. And the blood of Jesus washes not only your sin, but also that face of yours that does not dare to lift itself up.

The wounded heart says, "Why should it be me who goes first? He hurt me so deeply." Let me say this very honestly: the one who goes first really does carry more of the pain. Esau's running step cost him twenty years of resentment. But brothers and sisters, the One on the cross is precisely the One who was wounded most deeply and still came running first. The step you take first is the step in all the world that looks most like Jesus.
Four kinds of heart, one embrace. There is room in Esau's arms for the proud, for the fearful, for the ashamed and for the wounded — because behind that embrace stands the cross.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, towards God. Pick out that one name, and pray for him before God for seven days. Not asking God to change him — asking God to walk into his heart ahead of you, and asking God to tell you what your own part in this is.

Second, towards yourself. Write out on paper the script you have written for the other person — how he will be cold, which sentence he will say. When you have finished, add one line at the bottom: "I wrote this. He did not say it." Then tear the paper up.

Third, towards people. Make one real move: a message, a phone call, or an apology said to someone's face. No explanations, no conditions attached, and nothing like "but back then you also …" tacked on to the end of it.

Fourth, towards your daily living. Give back what you took all those years ago. It might be a word, a sum of money, a position, a title that belonged to someone else. Give back as much as can be given back — what Jacob gave back was the blessing.

Fifth, towards your calling. Check whether you have stopped at Shechem. In your heart you know where God told you to go, and you also know where you have parked yourself instead. This week, walk the first kilometre of that final thirty.

Sixth, tell it to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is someone I have not been in touch with for twenty years. Second: I discovered that what was really stopping me was not him — it was the script I had written for him. Third: I have decided to walk over first, because there is One who walked towards me first.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will no longer wait for the other person to speak first; I will be the one who walks over.
I declare that every script I have written for somebody else is torn up today; I will believe only that God has long since been at work inside his heart.
I declare that my portion is in Jesus and not in anybody's attitude; because God has dealt graciously with me, and I have enough.
I declare that I will not stop at Shechem; I will walk to the end of that last stretch of road God has told me to walk.
This week I am meant to "make a phone call I have put off for a very long time", and I genuinely cannot get the words out. What should I do?

Three very practical steps. First, write out beforehand what you want to say, as three sentences: one of admission (I was wrong about that), one of restitution (this is what I would like to make up to you), and one that puts no pressure on him (whether or not you reply to me, I will respect it). Second, choose a slot when you yourself are in a good state — not late at night, and not just after a row. Third, accept the worst outcome: he may be cold, he may not reply at all. What you get to decide is whether you open that door; you do not get to decide whether he walks through it. And if that relationship involves harm done in the past, find a pastor or someone you trust to prepare for it alongside you.
Jacob prepared a great deal for that day. But what actually happened was that his brother came running over.

And we are the same. We spend enormous effort in our relationships calculating, preparing, defending — when in fact the deepest reconciliation of all was never something we negotiated. There is One who ran towards us first. "While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." He did not wait for us to apologise first.

So the focus is on Jesus — not on myself, not on other people, not on my circumstances. Not I, but Christ. I can walk towards that person because he walked towards me first; I can bow because last night I had already bowed before him; I can give it away because in him I have everything.

May God bless every one of us this week with the courage to make that call we have put off so long; may our faces become the place where another person sees the face of God; and may we not stop at nearly-there, but keep walking all the way to the Bethel he has prepared for us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson home as a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ "A face that is willing to forgive makes a person think of the face of God." How does that sentence change the way you look at forgiveness?
2. ★★ He sent "my blessing" back. Why is repentance not only saying sorry, but also giving back?
3. ★ Grace arrives in a moment; change is a road you walk. What does that say to the expectation that one meeting will put everything right?
4. ★★ He said he was going to Seir, went to Succoth instead, and built a house there. Why is "nearly there" so often the most dangerous place of all?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (he is the one who should bow, not me), fearful (I am afraid that making the call will only make things worse), ashamed (I dare not face the person I wronged), wounded (I have waited years for him to come to me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ In your contacts list, who is the name you skip past? What is it that stops you?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing I most need to give back is …"
9. ★★ This week, towards whom will you take the first step? Say which way you will do it, and on which day.

Leader's reminder: this lesson will touch old wounds inside families and between co-workers. Do not require anyone to forgive on the spot, and do not let the group pass comment on the people who get mentioned. If the other party is involved in ongoing harm, affirm that keeping a distance is entirely legitimate.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, what have your children or your family seen in the way you order things? Which one concrete arrangement will you adjust this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or in your ministry, who is it that keeps being put at the front to take the wind?
12. ★★★ The practice of the slowest sheep: this week, in the group you lead, walk once at the pace of the slowest person. Say who that person is, and say what you will do.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and rehearse the call you are going to make by telling it to him first. Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there are two brothers in the Bible who fell out over a blessing and did not speak for twenty years, and the younger one was so frightened he could not sleep all night. Second, on the day they met, the elder brother came running out of the crowd and threw his arms around him, and the two of them wept. Third, and so I believe that a face willing to forgive makes a person think of God. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the name you keep skipping past, and the first step you will take this week. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to give us hearts that bow before him first, and then the courage to bow our heads before people.
